title: Development of Antimicrobial and Antioxidant Properties of Electron Beam–Irradiated Polyvinyl Alcohol/Carboxymethylcellulose Blend Using Tannic Acid-Mediated Nanosilver
abstract: Abstract Using a solution casting technique, electron beam-irradiated polymer nanocomposite films based on polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) were successfully produced and reinforced with silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) mediated by tannic acid (TA). Tannic acid acted as a stabilizing and reducing agent at the same time in this green synthesis method, allowing well-dispersed AgNPs to develop within the polymeric matrix. To improve interfacial interactions and overall performance, the produced films were then subjected to an electron beam irradiation dose of 25 kGy as an optimum dose. FT-IR, XRD, UV/Vis, TEM, and SEM techniques have been used to investigate structural, optical, and morphological characteristics. The development of a face-centered cubic silver phase is verified by the XRD characterization, indicating that tannic acid reduction was successful in generating silver nanoparticles. The majority of the nanoparticles were spherical, with an average size of 12.5 nm, according to TEM studies. The addition of TA-Ag NPs and electron beam irradiation treatment significantly improved the tensile characteristics of the nanocomposite films, as shown by mechanical testing. This improvement was ascribed to better intermolecular contacts and irradiation-induced crosslinking. The thermal analysis results indicate that the PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite films have enhanced thermal stability compared with pure polymeric film. This study investigated the antimicrobial activity of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag NPs films against pathogenic microbes of  Staphylococcus aureus , MRSA,  Proteus mirabilis ,  Proteus vulgaris , and  Candida albicans . The PVA/CMC films containing 10 mL of TA-Ag NPs were highly effective against  S. aureus  and  P. mirabilis  with inhibition zone diameters of 25.02 ± 0.45 and 25.80 ± 1.23 mm, respectively. At 500 µg/mL, the PVA/CMC/TA-Ag NPs demonstrated a noteworthy antioxidant activity of 56.86 ± 3.54%. These findings of combination electron beam-induced crosslinking of PVA/CMC films with tannic acid-mediated green synthesis of silver nanoparticles create a multifunctional nanocomposite with improved mechanical and thermal performance, enhanced structural stability, significant antioxidant activity, and broad-spectrum antimicrobial efficacy make them appropriate for several applications such as in packaging and medical settings.
journal: Journal of Inorganic and Organometallic Polymers and Materials

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The remarkable physical and chemical properties of nanocomposites, which result from the nanofillers’ intense interfacial reactivity and extraordinarily high surface-area-to-volume ratios, have attracted a lot of attention in recent decades. When a little amount of nanofiller with smaller dimensions than 100 nm is introduced to the matrix, the properties of the composite material change. On completely new scales, nanocomposties offer opportunities to overcome obstacles in the food packaging, electronics, pharmaceutical, medical, and energy sectors. The intrinsic properties of polymers, such as flexibility, mechanical stability, and corrosion resistance, are combined with the heat stability, chemical stability, and chemical resistance, as well as the optical, electrical, and antimicrobial properties of inorganic nanomaterials, to create a new class of materials called polymer nanocomposites [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ].

The development of nanocomposites based on blended polymers and nanomaterials has recently attracted the attention of numerous researchers due to their improved properties and numerous technological uses. Polymer blending is the process of combining two or more polymers to produce a new product with special qualities [ 4 ]. The blending procedure for polymers has received a lot of interest since it makes it possible to create new polymeric materials with some of the required properties of each component for specific uses [ 5 ]. Water soluble polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) is widely used semi-crystalline and synthetic polymer. Although its drawbacks include restricted barrier and thermal qualities and comparatively expensive cost, it is biocompatible, biodegradable, nontoxic, film-forming, transparent, odorless, and has good chemical resistance and high mechanical properties. PVA mixed with other polymers due to its low rate of biodegradation and comparatively expensive material cost. Additionally, PVA is highly compatible with a number of natural polymers, including cellulose-based polymers, starch, and chitosan, which can be used for packaging applications [ 6 ]. The majority of recent studies on environmentally acceptable polymeric compositions for food packaging have been on biopolymers. Biopolymers, which come from natural sources like microbes, plants, and animals, present a viable substitute for traditional plastics made of petroleum [ 7 ,  8 ,  9 ]. Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), a naturally occurring biopolymer, is combined with other biodegradable polymers, specifically PVA, which is a water-soluble polymer, to overcome the aforementioned drawbacks. One of the cellulose derivatives, CMC has a number of advantageous qualities, including being non-toxic, biodegradable, readily soluble in water, affordable, and having good film formation. For both intra- and inter-hydrogen bonding, the hydroxyl group (OH) in the chain backbone of PVA and CMC structures serves as a functional group. Because of the multifunctional groups in their macromolecular chains, blending PVA and CMC enhances their physical contacts and polymer network entanglement, producing high-performance packaging materials with superior mechanical qualities [ 10 ]. The addition of CMC to PVA to produce polymers with desired qualities and attributes has been the subject of extensive investigation [ 11 ,  12 ].

Metal nanomaterials have garnered a lot of attention lately due to their unique chemical and physical properties as well as their importance in technological applications. Because of its unique optical, electrical, photothermal, and biological properties that distinguish it from its bulk counterparts, silver is one of the most intriguing metal nanoparticles. Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) have shown remarkable progress in biomedical applications. AgNPs are an intriguing nanomaterial because they are easy to create, affordable, and have a low concentration immune response. Additionally, AgNPs demonstrated promising qualities for wound dressing, medication delivery, medical imaging, diagnostics, and antimicrobial qualities. Silver nanoparticles’ high sensitivity to oxidation and agglomeration significantly diminishes their antimicrobial and anti-biofilm characteristics, which affects their practical applicability. To address these problems, the AgNPs surface can be modified with surfactants, polymer molecules, or other modifiers to increase the overall dispersion of particles and their stability in aqueous conditions [ 13 ,  14 ,  15 ].

There are many synthetic approaches were employed in the preparation of AgNPs such as chemical, electrochemical, thermal and photochemical methods. Among the chemical reducing agents, silver nanoparticles synthesized using hydrazine, sodium borohydride, ethylene glycol, etc., may be related with toxic chemicals and hence find restricted applications. Green synthesis was employed to diminish the chemical wastage and to reduce the additional cost of chemical reagents [ 16 ]. Tannic acid (TA), a polyphenolic chemical originating from plant sources, has attracted a lot of interest as a green reducing agent for the synthesis of nanoparticles because it is known to be non-toxic and environmentally benign. Due to their reducing activity at ambient conditions, it offers a sustainable alternative to conventional synthetic methods of nanoparticle avoiding the use of hazardous chemicals or higher temperature. TA decreases the contribution of extra chemicals such as stabilizing or capping agents owing to its good chelation ability. TA is also known for unique biological properties. When combined with silver, tannic acid is expected to enhance silver’s well-known antimicrobial activity. Additionally, TA is compatible with both PVA and biopolymers [ 17 ,  18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 ]. Although the fact that PVA/CMC films containing silver nanoparticles have been reported in a number of research, the current study makes the combination of radiation engineering, polymer blending, and green nanoparticle manufacturing results in a mechanically improved, biologically active, and multipurpose nanocomposite film is demonstrated in this work.

Treating polymers with ionizing radiation, such as accelerated electrons and gamma rays, is an interesting way to improve polymeric materials. In polymeric matrices, exposure to ionizing radiation can produce excited species and primary and secondary free radicals. These events ultimately lead to the crosslinking and/or destruction of polymeric materials, depending on the radiation dosages absorbed. This approach is considered safe because it doesn’t use solvents or high-temperature starting ingredients. Additionally, the ionizing radiation approach sterilizes medicinal and polymeric items [ 22 ,  23 ,  24 ,  25 ,  26 ].

The main objective of the present study was to synthesize active nanocomposite films based on AgNPs and PVA/CMC biopolymer matrix by solution casting method. Silver nanoparticles were synthesized by a simple, cheap and one pot route using tannic acid as a reducing agent and stabilizing agent at room temperature, offering a more scalable and sustainable approach. The structural, mechanical, thermal, antioxidant, and antimicrobial properties of the nanocomposite films were examined.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Alpha Chemika Co. India provided the poly (vinyl alcohol) (88.24% Hydrolysis and M.Wt = 125.000 g/mol). El Nasr Pharmaceutical Chemicals Co. provided the carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC). Egypt. Nice Chemicals PVT.LTD, India, provided the silver nitrate. The supplier of tannic acid (TA) was ADVENT CHEMBIO PVT.LTD India. Throughout the experiment, double-distilled water was used. Every chemical and compound was of analytical grade and was utilized just as supplied, requiring no additional purification.

sections.heading: Preparation of Tannic Acid-Functionalized Silver Nanoparticles
paragraphs: A typical experiment involved dissolving 0.5 g of TA in 50 mL of distilled water at room temperature for almost half an hour using a magnetic stirrer. After that, 0.25 g of AgNO 3  was added to the mixture, and it was stirred for 30 min to make sure that TA and silver ions would undergo a substantial complexion reaction. Finally, the silver nanoparticles were formed through seconds and the solution turns to dark brown when the PH was adjusted to 8 using 1M NaOH.

sections.heading: Fabrication of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag Nanocomposites Films
paragraphs: A straightforward solution casting technique was used to fabricate the PVA/CMC polymer blend and its nanocomposite films. A magnetic stirrer is typically used to dissolve 3.2 g of PVA in 100 mL of deionized water at 90 °C until a clear, homogenous solution is obtained after about two hours. After allowing the PVA solution to cool to 70 °C, 0.8 g of CMC was added and dissolved in the PVA solution while being continuously stirred, creating a 4% PVA/CMC blend with an 80/20 ratio. The blended PVA/CMC solution was then continuously stirred while 3 g of citric acid (3%) was added as a crosslinker and a preservative. To enhance the qualities, 1 mL of glycerol was also added (as a plasticizer). Subsequently, varying volumes (0, 1, 5, and 10 ml) of TA-AgNPs suspension were added to the PVA/CMC solution to create PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite films, which were then stirred for one hour at room temperature to achieve a homogeneous distribution. Ultimately, the resultant nanocomposites solution was poured onto glass Petri plates that had been well cleaned and dried, and it was allowed to dry at room temperature in the open until the water solvent had entirely evaporated from the films (Fig.  1 ). The prepared films were stored by placing it in a desiccator in a desiccator with a relative humidity of 56.8% for 24 h at room temperature (25 °C) to confirm complete dryness before further analysis. The dried films were then exposed to different electron beam irradiation doses (0, 10, 25, and 40 kGy) at ambient conditions using the National Center for Radiation Research and Technology’s electron beam accelerator facility (energy 3 MeV, power 90 kW, beam current 30 mA, conveyer speed 16 m/min (50 Hz), and scan width adjustable up to 90 cm) [ 27 ,  28 ].
Fig. 1 The synthesis steps of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite films

sections.heading: Characterization of the Nanocomposite
paragraphs: The IR spectra of silver nanoparticles and nanocomposite films were achieved using Attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) Vertex 70 FTIR spectrometer. High-resolution Transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) observation was performed using a JEOL JEM-2100 F microscope (Japan) operating at 200 kV accelerating voltage. The surface morphology of polymer nanocomposites was showed by using scanning electron microscope apparatus (SEM, ZEISS EVO-15) running at a 30 kV acceleration voltage. The mechanical characteristics of polymer nanocomposites films were measured using tensile testing machine (Qchida computerized testing instrument, Dongguan Haida Equipment Co., Ltd., China). Thermal properties were evaluated based on both thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).The TGA analysis was performed using a Shimadzu TGA-50 (Kyoto, Japan) from 25 °C to 600 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C/ min under N 2  atmosphere with a flow rate of 20 mL/min. DSC investigations were tested using Differential scanning calorimeter DSC131 evo (SETARAM Inc., France) with a heating rate of 10 °C/min.

Antimicrobial and Antioxidant Activities of Nanocomposites
paragraphs: The bacteria  Staphylococcus aureus  ATCC 6538, Methicillin-resistant  Staphylococcus aureus  (MRSA) ATCC CC239,  Proteus mirabilis  ATCC 29,906,  Proteus vulgaris  ATCC 6380, and the yeast strain  Candida albicans  ATCC 2091, which were obtained from the culture collection of the Drug Microbiology laboratory, Drug Radiation Research Department, National Center for Radiation Research and Technology (NCRRT). The agar disk diffusion assay was used to evaluate PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposites against the bacteria. Agar plate surfaces were inoculated with bacterial inoculums of 4 × 10 5  CFU/mL. Disks of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite with a width of 6.0 mm were placed over the agar surface. The zone of inhibitions was found after the 24-hour incubation period at 37 °C [ 14 ,  31 ].

sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
paragraphs: The biological assays were performed in triplicate. The results of all tests of the biological efficiency were regarded as (Mean ± SD). The statistical examines were accomplished by one way ANOVA at  P  < 0.05. The antimicrobial results were recorded as least significant difference (LSD) and Duncan’s multiple range analyses employing the SPSS (IBM) software (V24).

sections.heading: Characterization of TA-Ag NPs
paragraphs: The UV–vis optical absorption spectra of PS and TA-Ag NPs are displayed in Fig.  2 . Pure TA was found to have an absorption peak at 280 nm, which corresponds to aromatic ring π-π* transitions [ 33 ]. Additionally, it is evident that an absorption peak at 420 nm corresponds to surface plasmon resonance (SPR), which is caused by the collective oscillation of free carriers in response to applied electromagnetic radiation. The location of this peak varies depending on the size and shape of NPs [ 34 ,  35 ]. The production of spherical and smaller AgNPs (< 30 nm) is typically implied by the SPR between 400 and 450 nm [ 36 ]. Figure  3  shows the XRD patterns of TA-Ag NPs. The XRD spectrum revealed five peaks at 38.05◦, 44.07◦, 64.37◦, and 77.25◦, which were identified as (111), (200), (220), and (311) silver crystal planes with a face-centered cubic (FCC) phase structure. The unique broad peak at 24◦ reveals the amorphous nature of TA [ 37 ], respectively according to (JCPDS card no. 4-0783) [ 38 ,  39 ]. This pattern shows that pure crystalline silver can be obtained and is free of contaminants. The Scherrer equation (D = 0.9λ/βcosθ), where λ = 0.154056 nm (X-ray wavelength), β is the peak full width at half maximum of the (111) peak (radians), and θ is the diffraction angle of this peak, was used to compute the average crystallite size (D) based on the most intense diffraction peak (111). AgNPs’ estimated crystallite size (D) is 8 nm.
Fig. 2 UV-Vis spectra of TA and TA-Ag NPs
Fig. 3 XRD pattern of TA-Ag NPs

FTIR analysis was used to examine the synthesized TA-AgNPs’ chemical composition. Figure  4  displayed the FTIR absorption spectra of TA and TA-AgNPs. The O–H stretching vibration may be responsible for the strong broad band that appeared in the TA spectra at about 3412 cm − 1  [ 40 ]. The stretching vibration of carbonyl compounds may be connected to the band at 1630 cm − 1 . The stretching vibrations of C–C in the benzene ring may be responsible for the peak at 1437 cm − 1 . The peak that emerged at 1368 cm − 1  may be associated with bending vibrations for O–H and C–H (in the benzene ring) [ 41 ]. The vibrational stretching of (C-O-C) and (C-O) with the phenolic compounds was responsible for the bands 1049 and 1089 cm − 1  [ 42 ].

The characteristic TA bands were seen in the TA-AgNPs spectrum, but with some noticeable alterations. As can be seen, the O–H stretching vibration shifts from 3412 cm − 1  to 3423 cm − 1  with a small decrease. Additionally, it is evident that the C = O band’s intensity increases with broadening, suggesting that the tannic acid-mediated reduction mechanism—in which the galloyl group in tannic acid changed from the phenolic form to the quinone form—was successful in forming and stabilizing silver nanoparticles [ 43 ,  44 ]. The released electrons in this process reduce silver ions, and the consumption of –OH groups increases the amount of carbonyl groups (Scheme  2 ). Furthermore, the vibrations of (N-O) of the precursor AgNO 3  utilized cause the peak at 1382 cm  − 1  to be more strong [ 45 ,  46 ].
Scheme 2 Transformation phenolic form of Tannic acid into quinone form and the reduction of Ag +  into Ag 0
Fig. 4 FTIR spectra of TA and TA-Ag NPs

Figure  5  displays the TA-Ag NPs’ particle size, shape, and morphology as determined by TEM. It is evident that the TA-Ag NPs have homogenous spherical-shaped particles and a limited particle size distribution. TA-Ag NPs feature a spherical structure covered in a light gray TA, according to a magnified TEM picture. The histogram of the TA-Ag NPs size distribution fitted with a Gaussian curve is attained as the solid lines in the figure with a mean diameter equal 12.5 nm. The narrow size distribution of TA-Ag NPs is confirmed by the obtained shape of Gaussian peak. This result is nearly consistent with XRD result. Additionally, the bright spots at regular locations in the Ag NPs’ selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern suggest their nano-crystalline structure, which is consistent with XRD studies.
Fig. 5 TEM images with different magnification with the corresponding histogram of the particle size distribution with Gaussian fitting and selected electron diffraction area of TA-Ag NPs

sections.heading: Swelling, Gel, and Atomic Absorption
paragraphs: Electron beam irradiation significantly influenced the swelling and gel fraction behavior of PVA/CMC nanocomposite films. The swelling percentage decreased from 150.7% in the non-irradiated film to 97.3% at 25 kGy due to radiation-induced crosslinking, which reduced chain mobility and free volume. At 40 kGy, swelling increased to 132.0%, indicating that chain scission began to dominate over crosslinking. On the other hand, the addition of tannic acid (TA)-mediated AgNPs further reduced swelling from 97.3% to 63.2% as TA concentration increased to 10 mL of TA-AgNPs as shown in Fig.  6 a. This reduction is attributed to strong hydrogen bonding between TA and the PVA/CMC matrix, enhanced radiation-induced crosslinking, and the filling effect of AgNPs within the polymer network. The resulting dense three-dimensional structure restricted water penetration and improved dimensional stability. Conversely, the gel fraction increased with irradiation dose, rising from 36.0% at 0 kGy to 59.8% at 25 kGy, confirming enhanced network formation through crosslinking. Increasing TA-AgNPs concentration further elevated the gel fraction from 59.8% to 78.2%, demonstrating the synergistic effect of TA-AgNPs and electron beam irradiation on network stabilization. TA acted as a multifunctional crosslinking mediator through hydrogen bonding and coordination interactions with AgNPs as shown in Fig.  6 b. The uniformly dispersed AgNPs also contributed as physical crosslinking sites.
Fig. 6 A  Swelling %, and  B  the Gel % of PVA/CMC films at different irradiation dose and PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposites films at optimum irradiation dose (25 kGy)

The extent of Ag nanoparticles leached out from the PVA/CMC matrix upon immersion in water was determined by using the atomic absorption measurement (GBC Savant AA atomic absorption analyzer, Australia). About minor traces of Ag ( 0.17, 0.27, and 0.45 mg/L for polymeric film containing 1 ml ,5 ml, and 10 ml TA-Ag NPs, respectively ) was determined after 4 h of soaking i.e. the Ag nanoparticles are tightly held within the polymeric chains. This could provide a perfect confirmation for the fixation of Ag nanoparticles within the crosslinked PVA/CMC polymeric chains and this result agree with Eisa et al. [ 47 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical Measurements
paragraphs: Figure  7  displays the mechanical characteristics of the PVA-CMC films with varying irradiation doses and TA-Ag NP concentrations. Tensile strength (TS) and elongation at break (E b %) are the mechanical characteristics that are being examined and the resulting values along with the thickness have been displayed in Table  1 . The mechanical behavior of CMC-PVA films treated to three irradiation doses 10, 25, and 40 kGy is shown in Fig.  7 a. It was shown that the TS rose as the radiation dose increased up to 25 kGy before declining at 40 kGy. The cross-linking of CMC-PVA films caused by radiation up to 25 kGy is responsible for the rise in TS. Meanwhile, the decrease in TS values at high irradiation dose, namely 40 kGy is due to degradation effect by radiation. Additionally, it was seen that the Eb% values decreased as the irradiation dose increased. This was explained by the creation of a radiation cross-linking network in the polymeric matrix, which limited the molecular chain’s mobility during drawing. However, the results showed that the TS increased with the addition of TA-Ag NPs up to concentration of 5 ml TA-AgNPs, and then it was decreased at 10 ml of TA-Ag NPs (Fig.  6 b). The results at low concentration of TA-Ag NPs are caused by an increase in the adhesion and interfacial contact between silver nanoparticles and polymeric chains [ 48 ,  49 ,  50 ]. Additionally, adding more TA-Ag NPs results to more TA residue that reacted with PVA and CMC as reported in the literature [ 51 ,  52 ]. This increases the cross-link density of polymers that include OH groups [ 53 ,  54 ]. The abundance of hydroxyl groups in the phenolic compounds develops stronger bonds with the polymeric matrix [ 55 ]. Also, as is the case with PVA-CMC films loaded by Cu-NPs, the hydroxyl and carboxyl groups in the blend are electrostatically linked to the TA-Ag NPs [ 56 ]. The presence of TA-Ag NPs causes hydrogen bonds to form between CMC, PVA, and TA, increasing the crosslinking density and raising the TS lowering. Eb% values. Conversely, at a high concentration of TA-Ag NPs (10 ml), the silver nanoparticles were agglomerates. This reveals weak interfacial regions that cause cracks, which reduce the efficiency of the stress transfer between the matrix and nanoparticles and eventually result in a reduction in the TS values of nanocomposites.

sections.heading: X-ray Diffraction (XRD) Analysis
paragraphs: X-ray diffraction analysis is used to further assess the effect of chemical change on the crystal structure. The X-ray diffraction analysis (XRD) patterns of PVA/CMC film and PVA/CMC/TA-Ag NCs nanocomposite films loaded with various TA-AgNP contents are shown in Fig.  8 . The semi-crystalline character of the PVA/CMC polymer blernd is responsible for the two large peaks that can be seen in the PVA/CMC film at 21◦ and 40◦ corresponding to the (101) and (111) lattice planes, respectively [ 57 ,  58 ]. Conversely, PVA/CMC/TA-Ag NCs nanocomposite films exhibit a minor extra diffraction peak at 2θ = 38◦, which represents the (111) plane of the silver nanoparticles’ face center cubic structure (FCC). The uniform coating of blend polymer on the AgNPs’ surface, their low concentration and fine dispersion in the PVA/CMC blend polymer may be responsible for the decrease in the intensity of the AgNPs’ distinctive diffraction peaks [ 59 ,  60 ,  61 ]. Additionally, the polymer blend’s diffraction peaks became more intense. The values of the degree of crystallinity were presented in Table  2 . The increase was attributed to the nanofillers effects which act as extra nucleating sites for the PVA/CMC blend polymer’s crystallization. This effect becomes more pronounced in the case of hydrophilic nanofillers, which can directly interact with the PVA /CMC blend polymer molecules through hydrogen bonding [ 62 ,  63 ,  64 ]. As shown in Table  2 , at higher concentration the degree of crystallinity is reduced compared to lower concentrations due to aggregation effect.
Fig. 8 XRD spectra of PVA/CMC polymer and PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite film containing different concentration of TA-AgNPs

sections.heading: SEM and EDX Analysis
paragraphs: The surface morphology of polymeric films before and after filling with Ag-nanoparticles at varying filling levels was investigated using SEM. Figure  9  shows SEM images of the surfaces of PVA/CMC polymer and PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite films at a magnification of 2000 times. The pure PVA/CMC polymer film has a smooth, fissure-free surface that is comparatively homogenous. Conversely, at a low concentration (1 ml TA-Ag NPs), white granules with sphere-like shapes of TA-AgNPs developed and were evenly distributed throughout PVA/CMC polymer. The compatibility of TA-AgNPs with the polymeric matrix is demonstrated by this observation. Little grain bunches developed and the polymeric nanocomposite’s surface became rough at greater contents. Additionally, there are no gaps or fissures surrounding the AgNPs in the membranes created, according to the SEM pictures. As had been addressed in the mechanical properties of nanocomposites, the agglomeration of TA-AgNPs nanoparticles at high concentrations, specifically TA-Ag (10 ml), results in the formation of large clusters rather than being uniformly dispersed. These clusters act as weak points, and cracks can initiate and propagate more easily from these regions, deteriorating the mechanical properties (TS) [ 65 ].

The elemental constituent in the tested samples was identified using the EDX technique. The element silver (Ag) in PVA/CMC polymer is confirmed by the EDX spectra, as seen in Fig.  10 , and the percentage of silver increases as colloidal silver nanoparticles are added. The emergence of the silver signal at about 3 keV has demonstrated the presence of silver nanoparticles [ 66 ,  67 ]. As can be seen, PVA/CMC polymer has no Ag, whereas the other PVA/CMC nanocomposites have weight percentages of 0.15%, 0.58%, and 0.98% for PVA/CMC/(1 ml) TA-AgNPs, PVA/CMC/(5 ml )TA-AgNPs, and PVA/CMC/(10 ml) TA-AgNPs, respectively.

Fig. 10 EDX analysis of  a  PVA/CMC polymer,  b  PVA/CMC / (1 ml) TA-Ag nanocomposite film,  c  PVA/CMC/(5 ml) TA-Ag nanocomposite and  d  PVA/CMC /(10 ml) TA-Ag nanocomposite film

sections.heading: FTIR Analysis
paragraphs: In order to identify the presence of significant chemical groups and their bonding inside a polymer matrix, FTIR analysis was investigated. Figure  11  presented the FTIR spectra of the pure PVA/CMC film before and after various TA-AgNP concentrations were added. The O-H stretching vibration, CH 2  stretching vibration, and C-O stretching vibration peak were identified as the major absorption peaks in the PVA/CMC blend sample’s spectra at 3295 cm − 1 , 2920 cm − 1 , and 1085 cm − 1 , respectively. The peak at 1725 cm − 1  is attributed to C = O stretching from the acetate groups still present on the PVA [ 68 ] and the carboxylic group of citric acid [ 69 ]. The peak at 1580 cm − 1  is associated with the carboxylate (COO – ) of CMC being stretched by C = O [ 70 ]. The stretching and vibration of the C-C bond are shown by the peak at 870 cm − 1  [ 11 ]. Conversely, the spectra of PVA/CMC/TA-AgNPs film show the same characteristics as PVA/CMC film, but the peaks’ intensities were altered. As demonstrated, the presence of TA moieties causes the OH and C = O peaks to broadning and intensify with the addition of TA-AgNPs [ 52 ]. This transition witnessed in OH absorption peak can potentially be ascribed to the establishment of hydrogen bond interactions between the carboxyl/hydroxyl groups in PVA/CMC polymer blend and the rich functional moieties in nanofiller (TA-AgNPs ) [ 71 ,  72 ].
Fig. 11 FTIR analysis of PVA/CMC polymer and PVA/CMC /TA-Ag nanocomposite film containing different concentration of TA-AgNPs

sections.heading: TGA and DSC Analysis
paragraphs: The thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) is a vital practical technique used to examine the thermal stability of polymers. The thermograms (TG) and the differential thermogravimetry (DTG) curves of PVA/CMC and PVA/CMC nanocomposite film containing different concentrations of TA-Ag NPs within the temperature range 25–600 °C are shown in Fig.  12 . As shown, these curves illustrate three distinct stages of thermal weight loss. The first stage, occurring below 200 ◦C, is due to moisture evaporation and the loss of low molecular weight compounds. The weight loss in this range was around 10%.The second stage, from 200 °C to 400 °C is due to main chain decomposition of PVA and CMC molecular chains followed by polyene formation, its weight loss around 70%. The third stage, between 400 °C and 600 °C, was caused by the degradation and carbonization of smaller molecular chain structures [ 10 ,  73 ]. It can be seen that the thermal stability of PVA/CMC nanocomposite film was enhanced by TA-Ag NPs addition.

The DSC analysis results for PVA-CMC blends and its nanocomposites loaded by different concentrations of TA-AgNPs are shown in Fig.  12 , also, the collected data results from this figure are shown in Table  3 . For the PVA-CMC blank film, DSC showed an endotherm melting transition (T m ) at 204.28 °C, representing the melting temperature of PVA-CMC. PVA/CMC/(1 ml) TA-AgNPs film exhibited an endotherm melting transition at 206.24 °C. The results also showed that the melting temperature of the PVA/CMC/(10 ml) TA-AgNPs film was increased and the T m  obtained at 213.746 °C. On the other hand, the melting Enthalpy, ΔH (J/g) was increased for nanocomposites by increasing adding of TA-AgNPs. These results can be explained by that Ag NPs provide a strong interaction with the polymer chains and restrict the mobility of the segments. These interactions make it difficult for the chains to move freely and require higher energy, i.e., higher temperature, for the polymer to soften [ 74 ,  75 ]. The interaction between polymer blend and TA-AgNPs lead to increase in T m  as obtained by similar data obtained for CoFe 2 O 4 /MWCNTs added to PVA-CMC [ 76 ].

sections.heading: The Antimicrobial Activities of the Prepared Nanocomposites
paragraphs: The antimicrobial activity of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite films at concentrations of 1, 3, and 10 mL TA-AgNPs was assessed qualitatively using the disk diffusion method. Several harmful bacteria were employed in this investigation. The antimicrobial activity of the prepared films is shown in Fig.  13 ; Table  4 , which show a markedly increased inhibitory effect against two Gram-positive bacteria,  S. aureus  and multidrug-resistant  S. aureus  (MRSA), two Gram-negative bacterial strains,  P. mirabilis  and  P. vulgaris , and the yeast strain,  Candida albicans , in comparison to those that did not include Ag NPs as a control. The neat film shows high inhibition due to the presense of citric acid which act as apreservative in the polymeric film [ 77 ]. Raising the concentration of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite films from 1 to 10 mL TA-AgNPs gradually affects all tested microbial strains, indicating that the antimicrobial activity of these films is concentration dependent. Ten milliliters is the concentration at which microbiological growth is considerably inhibited. Additionally, utilizing 10 mL of TA-Ag NPs in PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite films demonstrated strong antimicrobial effectiveness against  S. aureus  and  P. mirabilis , with inhibition zone diameters of 25.02 ± 0.45 mm and 25.80 ± 1.23 mm, respectively. With an inhibition zone diameter of 20.17 ± 1.69 mm, the PVA/CMC/TA-Ag films, on the other hand, are less effective at stopping the growth of MRSA when using 10 mL TA-Ag NPs.

Tannic acid stabilized silver nanoparticles have been shown in numerous studies to have antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. During their one-pot manufacture, tannin, an organic material that is biocompatible, was used as a stabilizer and reducing agent [ 78 ]. Numerous factors, including size, shape, surface charge, size distribution, particle morphology, and the reducing agents used in their manufacture, influence the biological impact of Ag NPs [ 79 ]. Tannic acid’s hydrophilic shell and hydrophobic moiety stabilized on Ag NPs play a crucial part in its ability to form bonds with bacterial cell surface proteins and lipid hydrocarbon chains. Ag NPs and the bacterial cell membrane can interact closely thanks to tannic acid’s polyphenolic characteristics [ 52 ]. The antimicrobial stability of Ag nanoparticles is widely recognized. Because of their nanomaterial characteristics, which include a large surface area and a very small partial size that enable them to easily infiltrate between sponge particles and survive for extended periods of time, Ag NPs are more effective and have a longer-lasting effect than conventional antimicrobial agents [ 80 ].

The antimicrobial efficacy of the PVA/CMC/TA-Ag NPs nanocomposite films presented in Table  4  is governed by a dual action of interfacial contact-killing and sustained active species release. When the hydrogel films interface with the moist microenvironment of the bacterial culture, the hydrophilic polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) networks undergo controlled swelling [ 81 ]. This moisture uptake acts as the primary gatekeeper for mass transport, enabling the internal oxidation of zero-valent silver (Ag 0 ) into bioactive silver ions (Ag + ). The released Ag+ ions diffuse out of the matrix into the surrounding agar, creating the distinct zones of inhibition observed. These ions bind strongly to the negatively charged thiol groups of bacterial membrane proteins, causing membrane depolarization and leakage. Concurrently, ultra-small Ag NPs that escape the swelling polymer network cross the cell envelope, inducing intracellular oxidative stress via the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which halts DNA replication and causes microbial cell death [ 82 ].

Biochemically, TA acts synergistically alongside the silver species rather than remaining an inert carrier (Long-Term Synergistic Antimicrobial, 2025). Phenolic hydroxyl groups are capable of chelating essential iron required for bacterial metabolism and directly precipitating bacterial cell wall enzymes [ 83 ].

The ionizing radiations have a crucial effect for sterilization and reduction of any remaining unreduced silver ions in the matrix. Simultaneously, the energy breaks down larger silver aggregates, promoting a higher density of much smaller, highly active Ag NPs within the polymer tracks. Smaller nanoparticles possess a vastly superior specific surface area, which dramatically accelerates the dissolution rate of bioactive Ag +  ions into the surrounding medium [ 84 ]. Furthermore, irradiation initiates free-radical crosslinking between the PVA and CMC chains. While a denser crosslinked network typically restricts macroscopic swelling, it creates a more structured, continuous pathway for controlled, prolonged ion diffusion [ 85 ]. This prevents a rapid burst release, ensuring a sustained, high local concentration of silver ions at the film-pathogen interface that effectively overcomes bacterial resistance mechanisms in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains [ 86 ].

sections.heading: The Antioxidant Activities of the Prepared Nanocomposites
paragraphs: DPPH radical scavenging analysis is used to evaluate the antioxidant effectiveness of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag films since it is a feasible and precise method [ 32 ]. The antioxidant properties of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite were evaluated at concentrations of 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 µg/mL. The common antioxidant was ascorbic acid, or vitamin C. The scavenging activity percentage is influenced by the concentration of ascorbic acid and PVA/CMC/TA-Ag NPs, as seen by the results in Fig.  14 . Consequently, the activity is found to increase with a progressive increase in concentration, peaking at a concentration of 500 µg/mL. As shown in Fig.  14 , the typical ascorbic acid exhibits scavenging activity of 84.63 ± 2.35%, while PVA/CMC/TA-Ag NPs have significant antioxidant activity of 56.86 ± 3.54%. The tannic acid’s phenolic concentration could be the reason for the high scavenging activity percentage.
Fig. 14 The antioxidant assay (scavenging activity %) of ascorbic acid and PVA/CMC/TA-Ag NPs at concentrations of 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 µg /mL using by DPPH radical scavenging

Antioxidants are synthetic or natural compounds that can stop or postpone oxidant-induced cell damage (ROS, RNS, free radicals, other unstable chemicals) [ 87 ]. The DPPH test is the most widely used technique for determining the antioxidant capacity of Ag NPs [ 88 ]. They hypothesized that Ag NPs’ enhanced antioxidant qualities result from polyphenols acting as antioxidants and Ag NPs acting as catalysts at the same time. The existence of functional groups on the surface of silver nanoparticles causes these characteristics [ 89 ]. Silver can exist in two oxidation states (Ag +  and Ag 2+ ) depending on the reaction conditions, and the resulting Ag NPs may be able to quench free radicals by donating or absorbing electrons, which explains the mechanism of silver nanoparticles’ antioxidant function [ 88 ].

Pure ascorbic acid functions as a freely mobile, low-molecular-weight reference that reacts instantaneously in solution but degrades rapidly when exposed to environmental oxygen, heat, or moisture [ 90 ]. Conversely, the antioxidant capacity of PVA/CMC/TA-Ag nanocomposite film is driven by the phenolic hydroxyl groups of tannic acid, which are immobilized within the crosslinked PVA/CMC polymeric network. For functional applications—such as preventing the rancidity of lipid-rich foods—a controlled, sustained radical-scavenging action is superior to a rapid, short-lived burst [ 52 ]. Recent studies confirm that composite biopolymer films achieving ~ 50–70% DPPH inhibition are fully sufficient to significantly halt lipid oxidation, delay weight loss, and extend the real shelf-life of fresh food products [ 91 ].

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Using a green synthesis method in conjunction with electron beam irradiation technology, a multifunctional PVA/CMC nanocomposite film reinforced with tannic acid-mediated silver nanoparticles (TA-AgNPs) was effectively created. A stable three-dimensional network with enhanced physicochemical characteristics was created by the effective solvent-free crosslinking method of electron beam irradiation (25 kGy). The effective production of crystalline face-centered cubic AgNPs with spherical shape and average particle sizes equal 12.5 nm was validated by structural analysis. Strong connections between TA-AgNPs and the PVA/CMC matrix as well as uniform nanoparticle distribution were shown by FTIR, SEM, and EDX studies. As demonstrated by a decrease in swelling from 150.7% to 97.3% and an increase in gel percentage from 36.0% to 59.8%, electron beam irradiation greatly improved network development. By raising gel content to 78.2% and decreasing swelling to 63.2%, the addition of TA-AgNPs further enhanced network stability, suggesting a synergistic impact between radiation-induced crosslinking and tannic acid-mediated interactions.

Because of increased interfacial adhesion, hydrogen-bonding interactions, and nanoparticle reinforcement, the produced nanocomposite films demonstrated increased mechanical strength and thermal stability. Additionally, the films showed outstanding biological performance, exhibiting broad-spectrum antibacterial action against  Candida albicans ,  Proteus mirabilis ,  Proteus vulgaris ,  Staphylococcus aureus ,  a nd methicillin-resistant  S. aureus  (MRSA). With inhibition zones of 25.02 ± 0.45 mm and 25.80 ± 1.23 mm against  S. aureus  and  P. mirabilis , respectively, films containing 10 mL TA-AgNPs showed the maximum antibacterial activity. Furthermore, at 500 µg/mL, the nanocomposites’ antioxidant activity reached 56.86 ± 3.54% DPPH radical scavenging. This work’s primary scientific contribution is the cooperative combination of electron beam irradiation processing and green tannic acid-mediated nanosilver production. This combined approach improves crosslink density, nanoparticle dispersion, in addition to improving network stability, dimensional stability, nanoparticle stabilization antibacterial efficacy and antioxidant functionality with simultaneously sterilizing the final material. The produced films have the advantages of environmental sustainability, active antimicrobial protection, antioxidant activity, and enhanced physicochemical stability when compared to traditional petroleum-based packaging materials.

Overall, the results show that PVA/CMC/TA-AgNP nanocomposite films exposed to electron beam radiation offer a suitable foundation for active food-packaging materials that can prolong food shelf life by inhibiting microbiological growth and oxidative deterioration. Additionally, they are appealing options for biomedical applications due to their broad-spectrum antimicrobial qualities. In order to support industrial application, future research should concentrate on food-simulation migration testing, real-world food storage assessments, biodegradation behavior, and scale-up production.
